newsitem.title: USA: 311-year-old adventurer's skull gets CT scan.
newsitem.headline: 311-year-old adventurer's skull gets CT scan.

text.p: A 17th-Century adventurer's skull was given a high-tech CT scan on Thursday as scientists tried to shed new light on the failed expedition of French explorer Rene Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle.
The skull, believed to be that of a crewman, was the only one found inside the wreck of La Salle's wooden ship La Belle, which sank off the Texas coast during a winter storm in 1686.

It was found when archaeologists excavated the two-masted La Belle from Matagorda Bay last October. Historians believe the La Belle's sinking changed the course of history in the New World by effectively ending French hopes of colonising what is now the southern region of the United States.

Doctors at the Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for children in Dallas carried out the CT (computerized tomography) scan on Thursday, projecting a three-dimensional image of the skull onto a computer screen and allowing experts to complete a physical reconstruction of the head and face in coming weeks.

"When you put a face to history, it becomes a lot more meaningful," said Wayne Smith, a research scientist at Texas A&M University and one of the archaeologists working on the artefacts and evidence found inside La Belle.

Smith said the skull was in very good shape and still contains a significant portion of brain matter because, like the wreckage of La Belle, it was buried and preserved in the fine silt of Matagorda Bay.

The model of the brain will be used by anthropologists to boost knowledge of 17th-Century man, and scientists also plan to take DNA samples from the skull and analyse its brain matter to find out more about the French crewman.

Smith told Reuters they already know he had an "incredibly painful" tooth abscess as well as a badly broken nose and a nasty gash on one side of his head, apparently the results of "one heck of an attitude adjustment fight".

"The CT scan and the models will provide more clues to the puzzle of who he was, what he looked like and what happened to him. We hope to eventually make a secure identification and return his remains to his descendants in France," Smith said.
La Salle explored the U.S. Great Lakes region in the 1670s and laid claim to half the continent in the name of France. He is credited with discovering the mouth of the Mississippi.

He mounted a new expedition from France in 1684, setting sail for what is now Louisiana with four ships. But one was lost to pirates, one broke up on a sand bar, another had to return home and only La Belle made it as far as Matagorda Bay.

La Salle went ashore and began leading land parties in search of the Mississippi. In January 1686, while he was on firm land, La Belle was caught in a winter storm and ran aground on a peninsula in Matagorda Bay, in part because the captain was drunk.
The loss of La Belle angered La Salle's mutinous crew and, when he set off for a French outpost in Illinois to seek help, they killed him.
Shortly afterwards Spain launched a string of expeditions to settle southern areas of what is now the United States, effectively blocking France's colonisation plans.

When they excavated La Belle archaeologists discovered muskets, trinkets, lead shot and detailed records of the ship's construction. The skeleton was found lying across a large coil of anchor rope, an unopened cask by its side.
